The overall declining mass transfer coefficient trend is descriptive of the physical mechanisms at play during drying as the sheet surfaces get dried, the evaporating front moves inside the sample thickness, and the internal liquid flow and diffusion control the overall mass transfer from the surface [Ramaswamy et al 1999]. The above experiments were repeated with other two basis weights of interest, namely 210 GSM liner board and 125 GSM corrugating medium. Interestingly, the three basis weight samples have distinct drying rate vs drying time behaviors, showing the clear differences between them. However, when the drying rates are plotted against the sheet moisture content, it shows a rather unique behavior, with all three basis weights showing a similar drying rate behavior. One of the key takeaways here is the activation of the falling drying rate regime. Irrespective of the basis weights and the pulp types studied, for unrefined pulp samples, the first falling-rate period begins approximately at X = 0.7 grams (g) water/grams (g) fiber zone. The conduction and convection heat and mass transfer results were compared against values from other literature experimental studies and were well within the limits of these studies, indicating a high applicability [Cameron et al. 2000, Ahrens et al. 1984, Wilhelmson et al 1995, Reardon et al 1998]. Independent experimental evaluation of heat and mass transfer correlations for drying of porous materials under relevant conditions also raised important fundamental differences with commonly used conventional flow over flat plate correlations and heat and mass transfer analogies. This is an important consideration for future modeling work on the drying of porous materials. Additionally, the physical properties of the dried paper samples were also evaluated following the TAPPI standards (TAPPI Test Methods. 1992], and these can be compared against other literature studies as well as studying the effect of novel drying methods and the use of auxiliary energies. Auxiliary Energy Applications RF Energy Applications A process intensification approach involving the integration of Radio Frequency (RF) heating, a volumetric electromagnetic technology, alongside traditional conduction and convection drying methods were next explored. Here again sensors were used to continuously monitor key parameters such as moisture content, supply system temperatures, sample temperatures, air flows, and drying rates in real-time. The effect of RF as an auxiliary energy source in localized environments at varying moisture levels was explored to optimize industrial drying systems, quantify potential improvements, and provide insights for future studies. Experimental results from trials combining RF with convection and with the base case alternating conduction- convection drying processes were then studied. Both microwave and radio frequency radiation are used to heat materials that are electrically non-conductive and composed of polar molecules.
